Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

appeal verb and noun

to a higher court or authority

also lodge an appeal, court of appeal, appeal against a verdict, right of appeal, allow an appeal, disallow an appeal

classical

Cic. Phil. 1.21 (Lewis & Short): ut dē majestāte damnātī ad populum prōvocent

prōvocō, prōvocāre, prōvocāvī, prōvocātum

verb, first conjugation; intransitive, ad + accusative of the court

appeal (to a higher court)

The Roman citizen’s appeal to the people against a magistrate, and so any appeal to a higher judge: ad populum prōvocāre. Its first sense is to call out, and to challenge (to a fight, a contest); Lewis & Short.

Other words

  • prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnis f. — an appeal

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Leg. 3.6 (Lewis & Short): ad populum prōvocātiō estō; Liv. 3.55 (Lewis & Short): est prōvocātiō, an appeal lies

    After Augustus also a challenge to single combat; in Christian Latin a spur or encouragement (Lewis & Short).

  • appellō, appellāre, appellāvī, appellātum — appeal to (a magistrate)

    verb, first conjugation; the magistrate appealed to in the accusative · also used · classical · Liv. 2.55 (Lewis & Short): Volerō appellat tribūnōs; Cic. Quinct. 64 (Lewis & Short): ā praetōre tribūnōs appellāre; Traupman 193: appeal (to), appellāre ad

    To call on a magistrate, classically the tribunes, for help against another; the noun is appellātiō (appellātiō prōvocātiōque, Liv. 3.56). Its everyday senses are to address and to name (see address).

  • appellātiō, appellātiōnis f. — an appeal (to a magistrate)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short s.v. appellātiō II: an appeal; Traupman 193; Cic. (Lewis & Short): intercessit appellātiō tribūnōrum; Traupman 272

Examples

  • appellātiōnem admittere

    to allow an appealTraupman 193

  • appellātiōnem improbāre

    to disallow an appealTraupman 193

  • jūdicium appellātōrium

    a court of appealTraupman 194

See also court, judge, trial, appeal.
